Mapped: Europe's largest data centre projects – and how they plan to get their power

The demands of AI are redrawing the data centre map of Europe – and where and how the new generation of gigascale campuses plan to get their energy is now a major issue for wind, solar and grid developers alike

In the week that the predicted AI boom made more headlines, the scale of its potential demands on Europe's power systems is underlined by this map of the 20 largest data centres under development on the continent.

Recharge teamed up with Denmark-based renewable energy research specialist Aegir Insights to produce the map, which is based on analysis of more than 4,000 data centres in Europe, drawn from a global database of more than 12,500 sites.

Hover over each development proejct to see details of what is known about its scope, schedule and how it plans to meet its power needs.

The largest on the list, the Paris AI Campus, is targeting up to 1.4GW.

For reference, the top ten largest data centres currently operating are also shown.

Recharge also spoke to Maria Ávalo Gadea, who leads data centre analysis for Aegir Insights, about some of her key takeaways from the map.

Most plan to lean entirely on the grid – but many don’t have an agreement

Of the 20 largest development projects identified by Aegir, nine are known to have a grid connection agreed. Ten of the rest either have an application pending or an unknown status. Connecting to the grid has emerged as the major headache facing Europe’s data centre industry. “A major problem is timing,” said Ávalo Gadea. A data centre can be built in in 18 to 24 months, but then the transmission connection typically takes seven to 10 years, and up to 13 in the most like congested markets.”

Self-supply is showing its face

While most of the 20 largest data centre developments will rely on the grid, two – one of Spain and one in Croatia – expect to rely on their own resources, either through behind-the metre solar and battery arrays or fuel cells. Two further projects combine grid supply with generation of their own, Ravenscraig in Scotland pairs its 550MW campus with a battery system, and Elsham Tech Park in Lincolnshire has consent for on-site power generation alongside battery storage.

AI is driving scale

It’s instructive to note that the largest data centre operating – the 255MW Marcoussis Campus in France – is half the capacity of the smallest project on the top 20 development list. The massive, expected demands of AI are driving development of gigascale data centre campuses across Europe. Compared to the demands of a ‘traditional’ co-location data centre, Ávalo Gadea said: “The story completely changes when we are talking about AI training, where the processors in a training cluster exchange data continuously throughout the run [but] the performance degrades as the physical distance between them increases.” Eighteen of the 20 projects on the top list are intended for AI development, she added.

Regulation is redrawing the data centre map

A glance at the map of largest data centre developments shows how two nations – the UK and France – account for many of them. Ávalo Gadea notes the absence from the list of what have been historically two of Europe’s key data centre markets, Ireland and the Netherlands. Both have been among the markets that have placed restrictions in the form of moratoriums, location or scale limits on the data centre sector in a bid to control strain on their power grids and other infrastructure. With the largest projects underway in both countries coming in at a few hundred megawatts, they fall below the scale of the top 20 list.

'FLAP-D' is changing

The development map also shows the evolution from the clusters of data centres in what the IT industry has traditionally called ‘FLAP-D’ – Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, Dublin. As well as the regulatory moves in Ireland and the Netherlands described above, the distinct nature of AI training, which can be carried out away from centres of data demand, and pressures on grids is driving some large new projects to Europe’s margins – for example in Scotland, the Nordics and Croatia.

The US is on another level

America’s red hot data centre sector is already running on a different level. "The five largest AI sites in the US already draw between 1GW and 2.2GW. Across 125 operational US sites that we have in our database, there are roughly 21GW running today," said Ávalo Gadea. “In other words, the 20 largest projects in Europe's development pipeline come to just over 15GW between them – less than the US already has operating in AI alone.

“The principal reason is likely speed to power. So US developers have made much greater use of generation built behind the meter and that lets them bypass connection queues, which is one of the main issues in in Europe.”
